description: Survey the vast diversity of the animal kingdom, from simple sponges to complex mammals.

slides.title: Welcome to Animal Taxonomy
slides.content:
# Animal Classification

Welcome to Animal Taxonomy! With over a million identified animal species, we need a rigorous system to categorize them based on their evolutionary relationships.

## What You Will Learn:
- **Principles of Taxonomy** - Binomial nomenclature and cladistics
- **Non-Chordates** - Invertebrates from sponges to starfish
- **Chordates** - The vertebrates, including us
- **Phylogenetic Trees** - Reading evolutionary history

> **Fun Fact:** Insects make up more than half of all known living organisms on Earth!

slides.title: Taxonomy and Phylogeny
slides.content:
# Organizing Life

## Linnaean Classification:
Developed by Carl Linnaeus. It uses a hierarchical system:
Domain -> Kingdom -> Phylum -> Class -> Order -> Family -> Genus -> Species.
*(Mnemonic: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup)*.

## Binomial Nomenclature:
Every species has a two-part scientific name in Latin: Genus (capitalized) + species (lowercase). E.g., *Homo sapiens*.

## Phylogeny:
Modern classification isn't just about what animals look like; it's about their evolutionary history. We use **Cladistics** to build phylogenetic trees, grouping animals based on shared derived characteristics (e.g., all mammals share the derived trait of hair).

slides.title: Basis of Classification
slides.content:
# How do we divide animals?

Animals are classified based on fundamental body plans.

## 1. Symmetry:
- **Asymmetrical:** No symmetry (Sponges).
- **Radial Symmetry:** Can be divided into equal halves in many planes (Jellyfish, Starfish).
- **Bilateral Symmetry:** Can be divided into left and right halves in only one plane (Insects, Humans).

## 2. Germ Layers:
- **Diploblastic:** Two embryonic layers (Ectoderm and Endoderm). e.g., Cnidarians.
- **Triploblastic:** Three layers (Ectoderm, Mesoderm, Endoderm). Allows for complex organs. e.g., Flatworms to Humans.

## 3. Coelom (Body Cavity):
- A fluid-filled space between the gut and body wall, entirely lined by mesoderm. Crucial for organ development and acting as a hydrostatic skeleton.

slides.title: Major Invertebrate Phyla - 1
slides.content:
# The Simpler Invertebrates

## Phylum Porifera (Sponges):
- Asymmetrical, multicellular but NO tissues.
- Body has pores (ostia) for water to enter and a large exit hole (osculum).

## Phylum Cnidaria (Jellyfish, Corals):
- Radial symmetry, diploblastic.
- Possess stinging cells called **cnidocytes**.
- Two body forms: Polyp (sessile, like corals) and Medusa (free-swimming, like jellyfish).

## Phylum Platyhelminthes (Flatworms):
- Bilateral, triploblastic, but **acoelomate** (no body cavity).
- Dorso-ventrally flattened. Many are parasites (tapeworms).

slides.title: Major Invertebrate Phyla - 2
slides.content:
# Complex Invertebrates

## Phylum Annelida (Segmented Worms):
- Earthworms, leeches. True coelomates with distinctly segmented bodies (metamerism).

## Phylum Arthropoda (Insects, Spiders, Crabs):
- The largest phylum. Bilateral, coelomate.
- Defining features: **Jointed appendages** and an exoskeleton made of chitin.

## Phylum Mollusca (Snails, Octopus, Clams):
- Second largest phylum. Soft-bodied, often protected by a calcareous shell.
- Defining features: A muscular foot, a visceral mass, and a mantle.

## Phylum Echinodermata (Starfish, Sea Urchins):
- Spiny-skinned marine animals. Adults have radial symmetry, but larvae have bilateral symmetry!
- Possess a unique water vascular system for movement.

slides.title: Phylum Quiz
slides.quizQuestion: Which phylum is characterized by having jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton?

slides.title: Phylum Chordata
slides.content:
# The Chordates

We belong to this phylum! All chordates must have four specific features at some point in their life cycle (even if just in the embryo):

1. **Notochord:** A flexible rod providing support (becomes the spine in vertebrates).
2. **Dorsal Hollow Nerve Cord:** Becomes the brain and spinal cord.
3. **Pharyngeal Slits:** Openings in the throat (become gills in fish, disappear in humans).
4. **Post-anal Tail:** A tail extending past the anus.

## Subphylum Vertebrata:
The notochord is replaced by a bony or cartilaginous vertebral column (backbone).

slides.title: Vertebrate Classes - 1
slides.content:
# Fish and Amphibians

## Class Chondrichthyes (Cartilaginous Fish):
- Sharks and rays.
- Skeleton is made entirely of cartilage, not bone.
- Must keep swimming to force water over gills (most lack gill covers/operculum).

## Class Osteichthyes (Bony Fish):
- Salmon, tuna, goldfish.
- Skeleton is made of bone.
- Have a swim bladder for buoyancy (they don't have to swim constantly).

## Class Amphibia (Frogs, Salamanders):
- "Dual life." Can live on land but MUST return to water to breed (eggs lack a protective shell and will dry out).
- Respire through lungs and their moist skin.

slides.title: Vertebrate Classes - 2
slides.content:
# Reptiles, Birds, and Mammals

## Class Reptilia (Snakes, Lizards, Turtles):
- Fully adapted to land. Possess dry, scaly skin to prevent water loss.
- Lay **amniotic eggs** (eggs with a leathery shell) so they don't need water to breed.

## Class Aves (Birds):
- Evolved from theropod dinosaurs. Defining feature: Feathers.
- Forelimbs modified into wings. Bones are hollow (pneumatic) to reduce weight for flight.
- Endothermic (warm-blooded).

## Class Mammalia (Humans, Dogs, Whales):
- Defining features: Presence of **mammary glands** (to produce milk) and **hair/fur**.
- Endothermic. Most give birth to live young (viviparous).

slides.title: Summary: Animal Classification
slides.content:
# Summary

## Key Concepts Reviewed:

- **Taxonomy:** Hierarchical naming based on evolutionary history (phylogeny).
- **Basis:** Classified by symmetry (radial vs bilateral), germ layers (diplo vs triplo), and coelom presence.
- **Invertebrates:** Porifera (sponges), Cnidaria (jellyfish), Platyhelminthes (flatworms), Annelida (segmented worms), Arthropoda (jointed legs), Mollusca (shells), Echinodermata (spiny skin).
- **Chordates:** Must have a notochord, dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and post-anal tail.
- **Vertebrates:** Chondrichthyes (cartilage), Osteichthyes (bone), Amphibia (dual life), Reptilia (amniotic egg), Aves (feathers), Mammalia (hair and milk).

> **Congratulations!** You have completed the Animal Classification module.
